scenes.notes: This session is about response time in generative AI applications and agents built on Microsoft Foundry. The main takeaway is that latency is a property of the whole request path, not of one model. In most agentic applications the time goes to two places: the number of tokens the model generates, and the number of model calls that run one after another before the user sees an answer. The deck starts with the fundamentals, then covers the features that shorten a single model call, then the agent-level choices (orchestration pattern, runtime, tools and protocols) that decide how many calls happen, and finally how to measure and govern latency. Each decision tree is a starting point and must be checked against evaluation results for the actual workload. All facts were checked against official documentation on 14 November 2026; preview features carry an asterisk. Model names are examples current at that date and change quickly. A likely question: is this specific to one model family? No. The levers apply across models; only the model names and per-model targets change.

scenes.title: Sources of latency in agentic applications
scenes.subtitle: One user turn adds up model calls, tool and retrieval waits, network hops and safety checks.
bar: Answer generation: time between tokens × generated tokens

cards.d: Each output token adds time; output length usually dominates one model call.
cards.detail: As per official documentation, the time for one model call is the time to the first token plus the time between tokens multiplied by the number of generated tokens. Output length is usually the largest single factor; each prompt token adds far less time than each generated token.

cards.d: Every planning, routing or hand-off step is another full model call.
cards.detail: In an agent, every planning, routing or hand-off step is another full model call that runs before the user sees an answer. The orchestration guide recommends the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets the requirement.

cards.d: Each tool call adds a round trip; tool definitions add prompt tokens.
cards.detail: Each tool call adds a round trip, and tool definitions add input tokens to every prompt. A small tool set, tool search on demand and parallel independent calls keep this part short.

cards.d: Gateways, middleware and cross-region calls add time to every request.
cards.detail: Every hop between client, web application, gateway, agent, model and tools adds time to every request. The baseline architecture recommends models in the same data region as the agents, and every hop must pass the stream through without buffering.

cards.d: Best-effort capacity varies more under high load; throttling adds retries.
cards.detail: Standard deployments are best effort and vary more at high, steady volume; throttling adds retries. The deployment type and service tier decide how consistent latency stays under load.

cards.d: Content filtering adds latency; the streaming mode decides when text is released.
cards.detail: Content filtering adds latency. With the asynchronous filter, tokens return at once while filters run in parallel; this suits lower-risk use cases where the client can remove text already shown.

scenes.principle: Use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets the requirement: a direct model call first, then a single agent with tools, and multi-agent orchestration only when needed.
scenes.notes: The key point is that one user turn is a sum of parts, and most of them run in series. As per official documentation, the time for one model call is the time to the first token plus the time between tokens multiplied by the number of generated tokens, so output length is usually the largest single factor; each prompt token adds far less time than each generated token. In an agent, every planning, routing or hand-off step is another full model call, and each tool call adds a round trip; tool definitions also add input tokens to every prompt. Network hops add time to every request, best-effort capacity varies more under high load, and content filtering adds latency too. The bar at the top is illustrative only; real proportions depend on the workload and must be measured. The design principle comes from the Azure Architecture Center guide to AI agent orchestration patterns: use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets the requirement. Sources: learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/latency and the agent design patterns guide. A likely question: which part is usually biggest? In chat workloads, generated tokens multiplied by the number of sequential model calls; a trace per user turn confirms it.

scenes.title: Four questions for a slow user turn
scenes.subtitle: Asked in order, cheapest changes first; each answer opens a deeper decision tree.

root.d: model calls, tool waits, hops and checks in series

measure.d: one trace per user turn  ·  p50, p95 and p99 with token counts  ·  timestamps at every hop

scenes.order: Order matters: buying capacity before reducing sequential calls and output tokens pays for time that design changes would remove.

questions.q: Can a model call, tool call or hop be skipped?

leaves.t: Direct model call when one call with the right context solves it
leaves.detail: The orchestration guide says that if prompt engineering can solve the problem, an agent is not needed. A direct Responses API call with grounding in the prompt is the fastest option.

leaves.t: Deterministic router instead of a chain of hand-offs
leaves.detail: When the specialist is known from the first message, route in code or with a classifier such as the Decisions API, instead of chaining hand-offs between large models.

leaves.t: Decisions API for classify, route or score steps
leaves.detail: For fixed-choice steps, the Decisions API returns a probability, a choice or a score instead of generated text. It is generally available since 22 October 2026, with gpt-6-luna.

Semantic caching in Azure API Management returns a stored answer for a similar prompt, so a hit skips the model call entirely. A miss pays for the embedding and lookup, and a similarity match can return an answer written for a different question.

questions.q: Can the first words reach the user sooner?
questions.d: Earlier visible text, same total work

leaves.t: Streaming end to end, without buffering
leaves.detail: Streaming does not change the total time, but the user starts reading at the first token. Every hop, including the web application and the gateway, must pass the stream through without buffering.
Tokens return at once while content filters run in parallel. The filter signal can arrive up to about 1,000 characters later, so the client must be able to remove text already shown.
The client renders tokens as they arrive and shows progress while the agent waits for tools, so the wait is visible rather than silent.
With reasoning models, a short preamble before deeper reasoning gives an earlier first visible text.
Open-ended work with no fixed plan fits background execution better than a chat turn: Responses API background mode and long-running hosted agents exist for that.

questions.q: Can each remaining call and wait be shorter?
questions.d: Fewer tokens, smaller models, leaner tools

leaves.detail: For short answers without multi-step reasoning, a small model such as gpt-5.4-mini at the lowest reasoning effort it accepts. Pick the smallest model that passes evaluation.

leaves.t: Lowest sufficient reasoning effort, capped output
leaves.detail: Output caps reserve less compute and stop generation earlier. For reasoning models the cap includes reasoning tokens; too low a cap can return no visible output. Reasoning effort none suits classification and voice.

leaves.t: Stable prompt prefix for prompt caching
leaves.detail: Prompt caching applies to prompts of at least 1,024 tokens whose beginning is identical; one changed character is a miss. The work is ordering prompts so that stable content comes first.

leaves.t: Small tool set, parallel calls, minimal retrieval effort
leaves.detail: Tool definitions cost tokens, so keep the tool set small or use tool search on demand. Independent function calls can run in parallel, and minimal retrieval effort skips query planning by a language model.
Hosted agents scale per session with no warm pool to configure. Keep start-up and readiness checks lean and consider memory snapshots; the debug latency header reports cold, warm or resume starts.

questions.q: Does latency hold at p95 under load?
questions.d: Consistent percentiles, not only a fast average

leaves.detail: Priority processing publishes latency targets per model and suits variable volume; provisioned throughput with spillover gives the lowest variance for steady, predictable volume.
Mixing workloads on one endpoint makes short calls wait behind long ones and lowers the cache hit rate.

leaves.t: Model in the same data region as the agent
leaves.detail: The baseline Microsoft Foundry chat architecture recommends deploying models in the same data region as the agents.

leaves.t: Throttling watched: 429 responses, spillover, service tier
leaves.detail: Watch 429 responses, spillover headers and the service tier returned in each response; priority requests can drop to standard on sudden ramps or peaks.

scenes.notes: This is the main decision tree of the story. Every slow user turn gets the same four questions, in order. First, avoid work: can a model call, a tool call or a hop be skipped altogether, for example with a direct model call, a deterministic router, the Decisions API or a semantic cache? Second, hide the wait: can the first words reach the user sooner through streaming end to end, the asynchronous filter, visible progress during tool calls or a short preamble? Third, reduce what remains: a smaller model, lower reasoning effort, capped output, a stable prompt prefix, a lean tool set and minimal retrieval effort. Fourth, keep it steady: priority processing or provisioned throughput, separate deployments and co-located regions. The order follows the optimization path: buying capacity before reducing sequential calls and output tokens pays for time that design changes would remove. Measurement frames the tree: a trace per user turn shows which question matters most, and latency budgets keep the gains. Each leaf opens a deeper decision tree from the deck.

scenes.title: Latency levers along the request path
scenes.subtitle: Request path of the baseline Microsoft Foundry chat architecture, with the main latency levers at each hop.

hops.detail: The client sends the request to the web application. It renders tokens as they arrive and shows progress while the agent waits for tools.

lev: Pass the stream through without buffering
hops.detail: The web application calls through the optional AI gateway. It passes the stream through without buffering and runs in the same region as the agent.

A gateway adds a hop to every call, so place it close to users and Foundry resources, and make sure it keeps streaming connections open. It can add a semantic cache, load balancing and a circuit breaker.

hops.d: Foundry Agent Service or Agent Framework
hops.detail: The agent runs in Foundry Agent Service or in Microsoft Agent Framework code and calls its model deployment and tools. Fewer model calls in series, compact context and iteration limits keep it short.
The baseline recommends deploying models in the same data region as the agents. Model size, output length, prompt caching and the capacity option decide the time of each call.

hops.d: Foundry IQ · AI Search · tool servers
lev: Small tool set, or tool search
Model Context Protocol (MCP) approval only where needed
hops.detail: The agent calls tools and knowledge sources such as Foundry IQ, Azure AI Search or MCP servers. The baseline recommends keeping the number of tools small and tracking agent and tool latency in Application Insights.

scenes.notes: This diagram follows the request path of the baseline Microsoft Foundry chat reference architecture in the Azure Architecture Center, simplified to the hops that matter for latency; security components are left out and the AI gateway comes from the generative AI gateway guide. Step 1: the client sends the request to the web application on App Service. Step 2: the web application calls through the optional AI gateway in Azure API Management. Step 3: the gateway forwards the call to the agent, which runs in Foundry Agent Service or in Microsoft Agent Framework code. Step 4: the agent calls its model deployment. Step 5: the agent calls tools and knowledge sources such as Foundry IQ, Azure AI Search or MCP servers. The baseline recommends deploying models in the same data region as the agents, keeping the number of tools small, and tracking agent and tool latency in Application Insights. A gateway adds a hop to every call, so place it close to users and Foundry resources, and make sure it keeps streaming connections open. A likely question: does a gateway slow responses down? It adds a hop, usually small compared with generation time, if nothing buffers the stream.

scenes.subtitle: One model call split into first-token time and generation time, with the Azure Monitor metric for each part.

metrics: Generation speed across models and capacity
Duration of the whole model call
reading: p50, p95 and p99, not averages
client, network and application time come on top
scenes.notes: This slide gives the vocabulary for the rest of the deck. Time to first token covers queueing and prompt processing; generation time is the time between tokens multiplied by the generated tokens; time to last token is the sum. Streaming does not change the total time, but it lets the user start reading at the first token, which is why first-token time is the right responsiveness metric for chat. Azure Monitor exposes these as Time to Response, Time Between Tokens, Time to Last Byte and Normalized Time to First Byte; the normalized metric is only for comparing across prompt sizes. Official documentation recommends always pairing a latency metric with a token-count metric, and percentiles describe user experience better than averages. These metrics are measured at the service, so client, network and application time come on top. Source: learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/openai/monitor-openai-reference. A likely question: why does a client test show more time than Azure Monitor? The gap is network, gateway and application time, which only a trace across every hop reveals.

scenes.title: Model-call optimization features
scenes.subtitle: Four ways to shorten one model call: reuse the prompt prefix, release text earlier, generate less, reason less.

b: On by default for GPT-4o and newer models
prompt_cache_key groups requests that share a prefix
Extended retention (24 hours) on supported models
panels.detail: Prompt caching applies to prompts of at least 1,024 tokens whose beginning is identical; one changed character is a miss. Hits show as cached tokens in the usage data, and in-memory caches usually clear after five to ten minutes of inactivity.

b: Default: text in chunks, after filtering
Asynchronous: text at once; filter signal follows
Trade-off: earlier text versus real-time vetting; suited to lower-risk use cases
panels.detail: Streaming with the asynchronous filter returns tokens at once while content filters run in parallel. The filter signal can arrive up to about 1,000 characters later, so the client must be able to remove text already shown.

b: Predicted outputs* for edits to known text
panels.detail: Output caps reserve less compute and stop generation earlier. Predicted outputs is in preview, for Chat Completions with GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 models.

b: none: latency-critical work such as classification and voice
Output caps include reasoning tokens; too low a cap can return no visible text
A short preamble before deeper reasoning gives an earlier first visible text
panels.detail: More reasoning effort means more reasoning tokens and longer calls; supported values vary by model. For reasoning models the cap is max_completion_tokens or max_output_tokens, and it includes reasoning tokens.

scenes.notes: These four features shorten a single model call. Prompt caching applies to prompts of at least 1,024 tokens whose beginning is identical; one changed character is a miss. It is on by default for supported models, hits show as cached tokens in the usage data, and in-memory caches usually clear after five to ten minutes of inactivity. The prompt_cache_key parameter groups requests that share a prefix on GPT-5.6 and later, and extended 24-hour retention exists for several GPT-5 and GPT-4.1 models. Streaming with the asynchronous filter returns tokens at once while content filters run in parallel; the filter signal can arrive up to about 1,000 characters later, so the client must be able to remove text already shown. Output caps reserve less compute and stop generation earlier. For reasoning models the cap is max_completion_tokens or max_output_tokens, and it includes reasoning tokens; too low a cap can return no visible output. Reasoning effort none suits classification and voice. Predicted outputs is in preview, for Chat Completions with GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 models. A likely question: does prompt caching need code changes? No. The work is ordering prompts so that stable content comes first.

scenes.title: Deployment and capacity options
scenes.subtitle: The deployment type and service tier decide how consistent latency stays under load.
rows: Best effort; more variability at high, steady volume
Any region, a data zone, or one geography
Latency targets per model; can drop to standard on sudden ramps or peaks
Pay per token at the priority rate
Global Standard or US Data Zone Standard only
Dedicated capacity; lowest latency variance; overflow to standard
Variable; can be rejected when capacity is unavailable
Any region or a data zone
Offline jobs with no user waiting
band: Provisioned throughput for the steady base load  ·  spillover to a standard deployment for overflow  ·  priority processing alongside provisioned capacity
scenes.notes: The deployment type and service tier decide how consistent latency is under load, not the raw speed of the model. Standard deployments are best effort and vary more at high, steady volume. Priority processing uses the same quota as standard and publishes latency targets per model, for example 99 percent of five-minute windows above 100 tokens per second for gpt-5.4-mini. It is enabled per deployment or per request with the service_tier parameter. Requests can drop to standard after a ramp of more than 50 percent in tokens per minute within 15 minutes, at peak demand, or for long-context requests; the response shows which tier served it. Provisioned throughput gives dedicated capacity and the lowest variance; spillover sends overflow to a standard deployment in the same resource and is recommended for global and data zone provisioned deployments. Flex processing, in preview, costs 50 percent less than standard but has no latency target and no automatic fallback. Batch has a 24-hour target. A likely question: can priority processing run in the EU data zone? Not today. It supports Global Standard and US Data Zone Standard only, so EU data zone workloads use provisioned capacity with spillover.

scenes.title: Model selection decision tree
scenes.subtitle: Four questions lead from the workload to a model choice; the first Yes decides.

qs.q: Spoken, real-time conversation?
qs.t: Voice Live API or Realtime API
qs.s: speech in and out; WebRTC for client audio
qs.detail: Real-time speech has its own stack: the Realtime API over WebRTC, which official documentation recommends over WebSockets for client audio, or the Voice Live API, a managed speech-to-speech service for voice agents.

qs.q: Fixed-choice answer: classify, route or score?
qs.s: a probability or a choice instead of generated text
qs.detail: For fixed-choice steps such as classification or routing, the Decisions API returns a probability, a choice or a score instead of generated text. It is generally available with gpt-6-luna. Microsoft-Decision-1, in preview, is a separate decision model designed for lower-latency, lower-cost workflows.

qs.q: Short answer without multi-step reasoning?
qs.s: for example gpt-5.4-mini; reasoning effort none
qs.detail: For short answers without multi-step reasoning, use a small model such as gpt-5.4-mini at the lowest reasoning effort it accepts.

qs.q: Prompt difficulty varies widely?
qs.s: Balanced or Cost routing mode over a model subset
qs.detail: Model Router picks a model per prompt. The routing decision adds a negligible share of inference time, but the Well-Architected guidance notes that routers add variability, so evaluate against a baseline.

other.t: Reasoning model at the lowest sufficient effort
other.s: cap output tokens; short preamble before reasoning
other.detail: Otherwise use a reasoning model at the lowest effort that passes evaluation, with capped output and a short preamble before deeper reasoning.

items: same prompts, model versions and percentiles
small models for routing, extraction, formatting
output caps, low verbosity, stop sequences
trained on examples from a larger model
per-model latency targets with priority processing

scenes.notes: Read the tree from the top; the first Yes decides. Real-time speech has its own stack: the Realtime API over WebRTC, which official documentation recommends over WebSockets for client audio, or the Voice Live API, a managed speech-to-speech service for voice agents. For fixed-choice steps such as classification or routing, the Decisions API returns a probability, a choice or a score instead of generated text; it is generally available with gpt-6-luna. Microsoft-Decision-1, in preview, is a separate decision model designed for lower-latency, lower-cost workflows. For short answers without multi-step reasoning, use a small model such as gpt-5.4-mini at the lowest reasoning effort it accepts. When prompt difficulty varies widely, Model Router picks a model per prompt; the routing decision adds a negligible share of inference time, but the Well-Architected guidance notes that routers add variability, so evaluate against a baseline. Otherwise use a reasoning model at the lowest effort that passes evaluation. Fine-tuning a smaller model on examples from a larger one is a documented way to cut cost and latency. A likely question: always pick the smallest model? Pick the smallest one that passes evaluation.

scenes.title: Capacity selection decision tree
scenes.subtitle: Four questions lead from traffic shape and data location to a deployment type and service tier.

qs.q: No user waiting for the answer?
qs.s: lower cost; no latency target
qs.detail: If no user waits for the answer, use Batch or Flex processing: both cost less than standard and have no latency target. Flex processing is in preview and has no automatic fallback.

qs.q: Data must stay in the EU data zone or one geography?
qs.t: Provisioned in that zone, with spillover
qs.s: priority processing is not offered on these types
qs.detail: Priority processing supports Global Standard and US Data Zone Standard only, so the documented option for consistent latency in the EU data zone or one geography is Data Zone or Regional provisioned throughput with spillover.

qs.q: Steady, predictable volume with a latency target?
qs.s: reserved capacity; overflow goes to standard
qs.detail: Provisioned throughput gives dedicated capacity and the lowest variance; spillover sends overflow to a standard deployment in the same resource. For models before GPT-6, cached input tokens do not consume provisioned capacity.

qs.q: Variable volume with a latency target?
qs.s: per deployment, or per request with service_tier
qs.detail: Priority processing uses the same quota as standard and publishes latency targets per model. Requests can drop to standard after a sudden ramp, at peak demand or for long-context requests; the response shows which tier served it.

other.detail: Everything else starts on Global Standard with separate deployments per workload, because mixing workloads on one endpoint makes short calls wait behind long ones and lowers the cache hit rate.

items: short calls never queue behind long ones
model in the same data region as the agent
tiers and targets differ per model
do not consume provisioned capacity before GPT-6

scenes.notes: This tree turns traffic shape and data location into a deployment type and service tier. If no user waits for the answer, use Batch or Flex processing: both cost less than standard and have no latency target. If inference must stay in the EU data zone or in one geography, priority processing is not offered on those deployment types, so the documented option for consistent latency is Data Zone or Regional provisioned throughput with spillover. Steady, predictable volume with a latency target also points to provisioned throughput; for models before GPT-6, cached input tokens do not consume provisioned capacity. Variable volume with a latency target suits priority processing, enabled per deployment or per request. Everything else starts on Global Standard with separate deployments per workload, because mixing workloads on one endpoint makes short calls wait behind long ones and lowers the cache hit rate. Whatever the choice, keep the model in the same data region as the agent and watch 429 responses, spillover headers and the service tier returned in each response. A likely question: can priority and provisioned capacity be combined? Yes. Official documentation describes provisioned capacity for the steady base and priority processing alongside it.

scenes.title: Orchestration patterns and sequential model calls
scenes.subtitle: Each step along the complexity spectrum adds model calls in series and widens the latency spread.

cols.detail: If one model call with the right context solves the task, a direct Responses API call is the fastest option; no agent is needed.

cols.cap: Often the right default; cap iterations
cols.detail: A single agent with tools is often the right default for enterprise use cases; set iteration limits to avoid tool-call loops.

cols.calls: one or more per stage, in order
cols.cap: No parallelism; avoid for independent stages
cols.detail: Sequential orchestration has no parallelism, so avoid it when stages are independent.

cols.calls: in parallel; slowest agent sets the time
cols.detail: Concurrent orchestration reduces overall run time, but the slowest agent sets the pace and model quota can make parallel work inefficient.

cols.cap: Avoid when the route is clear from the input
cols.detail: Hand-off adds a model call for every transfer; when the right agent is clear from the first input, a deterministic router or a simple dispatcher is better.

cols.cap: Slow to converge; avoid for time-sensitive work
cols.detail: Group chat should stay at three or fewer agents and does not fit real-time requirements. Magentic orchestration focuses on building and debating plans, not on speed, and is slow to converge.

scenes.arrow: MORE COORDINATION  ·  MORE MODEL CALLS IN SERIES  ·  LONGER AND MORE VARIABLE LATENCY
band: A model per agent matched to its task  ·  only the context the next agent needs  ·  iteration limits  ·  instrumentation of every hand-off
scenes.notes: The Azure Architecture Center describes a complexity spectrum: a direct model call, a single agent with tools, and multi-agent orchestration. Each step adds coordination overhead, latency and cost. A single agent with tools is often the right default for enterprise use cases; set iteration limits to avoid tool-call loops. Sequential orchestration has no parallelism, so avoid it when stages are independent. Concurrent orchestration reduces overall run time, but the slowest agent sets the pace and model quota can make parallel work inefficient. Hand-off adds a model call for every transfer; when the right agent is clear from the first input, a deterministic router or a simple dispatcher is better. Group chat should stay at three or fewer agents and does not fit real-time requirements. Magentic orchestration focuses on building and debating plans, not on speed, and is slow to converge, so avoid it for time-sensitive work. Antipatterns include overlooking multi-hop latency, adding agents without real specialization and letting context windows grow. Microsoft Agent Framework implements all five patterns with streaming and checkpointing. A likely question: when is multi-agent worth it? When specialization or security boundaries require it and evaluation shows a quality gain that justifies the extra time.

scenes.title: Orchestration pattern decision tree
scenes.subtitle: Five questions lead from the task to the simplest pattern that meets it; the first Yes decides.

qs.q: One model call with the right context solves it?
qs.s: Responses API with grounding in the prompt
qs.detail: If one model call with the right context solves the task, a direct Responses API call is the fastest option; the orchestration guide says that if prompt engineering can solve the problem, an agent is not needed.

qs.q: One domain, and its tools cover the work?
qs.s: often the right default for enterprise use cases
qs.detail: If one domain and its tools cover the work, a single agent with tools is the default; set iteration limits on tool rounds.

qs.q: Specialist known from the first message?
qs.s: code or a classifier, not a chain of hand-offs
qs.detail: If the specialist is known from the first message, route deterministically, in code or with a classifier such as the Decisions API, instead of chaining hand-offs between large models.

qs.q: Independent subtasks?
qs.s: subtasks in parallel, results aggregated
qs.detail: Independent subtasks run concurrently and the results are aggregated; the slowest agent sets the pace.

qs.q: Fixed, ordered stages?
qs.s: each stage gets only the context it needs
qs.detail: Fixed, ordered stages run sequentially, with each stage receiving only the context it needs.

other.s: open-ended work; background run, not a chat turn
other.detail: Open-ended work with no fixed plan is where group chat and magentic orchestration belong. Those runs fit background execution better than a chat turn: Responses API background mode and long-running hosted agents exist for that.

items: on tool rounds, hand-offs and review loops
only what the next agent needs

scenes.notes: This tree applies the complexity spectrum, so always start at the top. If one model call with the right context solves the task, a direct Responses API call is the fastest option; the orchestration guide says that if prompt engineering can solve the problem, an agent is not needed. If one domain and its tools cover the work, a single agent with tools is the default. If the specialist is known from the first message, route deterministically, in code or with a classifier such as the Decisions API, instead of chaining hand-offs between large models. Independent subtasks run concurrently; fixed, ordered stages run sequentially, with each stage receiving only the context it needs. Open-ended work with no fixed plan is where group chat and magentic orchestration belong, and those runs fit background execution better than a chat turn: Responses API background mode and long-running hosted agents exist for that. For any multi-agent design, the guide recommends a model per agent matched to task complexity, compaction between agents, iteration limits and instrumentation of every hand-off. A likely question: is hand-off ever right for chat? Yes, when the route truly depends on the conversation, with iteration limits and loop detection in place.

scenes.title: Agent runtime and framework decision tree
scenes.subtitle: Four questions lead from the chosen pattern to where the agent runs and what builds it.

qs.q: Instructions, a model and built-in tools are enough?
qs.t: Prompt agent in Foundry Agent Service
qs.s: Foundry runs the tool loop and keeps the state
qs.detail: A prompt agent in Foundry Agent Service runs on the Responses API-based runtime: the service handles tool loops and conversation state, and Foundry manages autoscale. There is no client round trip per tool.

qs.q: Multi-step tool, file or command work, run by Foundry?
qs.t: Prompt agent with the Copilot harness*
qs.s: Microsoft Copilot harness, chosen at creation
qs.detail: The Microsoft Copilot harness, in preview, is a managed runtime for prompt agents that need multi-step tool, file or command work; it is chosen when the agent is created.

qs.q: Agent must run inside existing application compute?
qs.t: Microsoft Agent Framework in the app
qs.s: Foundry Models as the model client
qs.detail: When the agent must live inside existing application compute, Microsoft Agent Framework runs in the application with Foundry Models as the model client. Agent Framework streams in every orchestration pattern.

qs.q: Real-time voice over one connection?
qs.s: Invocations over WebSocket; frames not buffered
qs.detail: For real-time voice, hosted agents offer Invocations over WebSocket, a full-duplex connection that passes frames through without buffering.

other.s: Agent Framework or other framework in a container
other.detail: Other custom orchestration fits a hosted agent, generally available since July 2026. Hosted agents scale per session with no warm pool to configure; keep start-up and readiness checks lean, and the x-ms-debug-latency-enabled header reports cold, warm or resume starts.

items: server-side tool loop; no client round trip per tool
per-session start; lean start-up and readiness
debug header reports cold, warm or resume

scenes.notes: This tree decides where the agent runs and what builds it, once the pattern is known. A prompt agent in Foundry Agent Service runs on the Responses API-based runtime: the service handles tool loops and conversation state, and Foundry manages autoscale. The Microsoft Copilot harness, in preview, is a managed runtime for prompt agents that need multi-step tool, file or command work; it is chosen when the agent is created. When the agent must live inside existing application compute, Microsoft Agent Framework runs in the application with Foundry Models as the model client; version 1.0 shipped in April 2026, and Python 1.26.0 and .NET 1.28.0 are current in November 2026. For real-time voice, hosted agents offer Invocations over WebSocket, a full-duplex connection that passes frames through without buffering. Other custom orchestration fits a hosted agent, generally available since July 2026. Hosted agents scale per session with no warm pool to configure, and the x-ms-debug-latency-enabled header reports cold, warm or resume starts. Workflows in the Foundry portal are in preview and retire on 1 December 2026. A likely question: do hosted agents have cold starts? Yes. Keep start-up and readiness checks lean, and consider memory snapshots.

scenes.title: Tools, protocols and retrieval decision tree
scenes.subtitle: Five questions lead from what the agent needs to a tool type, with the setting that matters for latency.

qs.q: Grounding on indexed enterprise content?
qs.s: minimal retrieval effort; extractive output
qs.detail: A Foundry IQ knowledge base uses agentic retrieval. Minimal retrieval reasoning effort skips query planning by a language model and gives the lowest latency; low, the default, adds planning, and medium can add one follow-up iteration. Low, medium and answer synthesis are in preview; extractive output is recommended for agents.

qs.q: Logic lives in the application code?
qs.s: application runs it; independent calls in parallel
qs.detail: Function calling keeps logic in the application, and independent calls can run in parallel.

qs.q: Tool shared by many agents or teams?
qs.s: approval only where needed; tool search
qs.detail: MCP approval defaults to always, and each approval adds a round trip, so set never or a per-tool list for trusted tools. An empty allowed-tools list allows every tool, and tool search, generally available since September 2026, exposes tools on demand to save tokens.

qs.q: Existing REST API with an OpenAPI description?
qs.s: return only the fields the agent needs
qs.detail: OpenAPI tools call existing REST APIs; returning only the fields the agent needs keeps the prompt small.

qs.q: Another agent owns the whole task?
qs.s: adds the other agent's own model calls
qs.detail: The Agent2Agent tool hands over a whole task; the called agent runs its own model calls, and Foundry agent targets support text only, without streaming.

other.s: web search, file search, code interpreter
other.detail: Otherwise the built-in tools of Foundry Agent Service cover web search, file search and code interpreter.

scenes.title: Latency observability and budgets
scenes.subtitle: One trace per user turn shows where the time goes; budgets turn percentiles into release gates.
scenes.caption: OpenTelemetry spans with token usage, stored in Application Insights.
monitor: p50, p95 and p99 per agent and model
band: p50, p95 and p99 targets per user journey and pattern  ·  release gates that fail on regressions  ·  evaluations rerun when a model or prompt changes
scenes.notes: A trace per user turn is the only way to see where time goes across hops. Microsoft Agent Framework emits OpenTelemetry spans by default, following the generative AI semantic conventions: invoke_agent for the run, chat for each model call and execute_tool for each tool call, with token usage as attributes; trace context also reaches MCP servers. Foundry tracing is generally available for prompt and hosted agents and stores spans in Application Insights. The agent monitoring dashboard, in preview, shows latency, token usage, run success rate and evaluation results; official documentation notes that run latency above ten seconds can point to throttling, complex tool calls or network issues. Insights, also in preview, groups recurring trace behaviour, including latency findings. Monitor first-token percentiles, generation time next to token counts, model calls per turn, tool span durations, cache hits and throttling. Then set a budget: p50, p95 and p99 targets per user journey and pattern, with release gates that fail on regressions and evaluations that rerun when a model or prompt changes. A likely question: is extra tooling needed? No. Connect Application Insights to the Foundry project and enable tracing in the framework.

scenes.title: Comparison of caching and capacity features
scenes.subtitle: Four features often confused, asked the same six questions.
rows: Reuses processing of an identical prompt prefix
Returns a stored answer for a similar prompt
Serves requests in a faster lane
API Management with Azure Managed Redis
Shorter first-token time on a hit
No model call on a hit; small overhead on a miss
May reuse an answer written for another prompt
Lower cost for cached input tokens
Fewer model calls; adds embeddings and a cache
Long, stable instructions and tool definitions
band: Prompt caching on every call  ·  semantic caching where answers repeat  ·  one capacity option for the latency target
scenes.notes: These four features are often grouped together as ways to go faster, but they work at different layers. Prompt caching reuses the processing of an identical prompt prefix inside the model service; the answer is still generated for every request, and the saving is in first-token time and input cost. Semantic caching in Azure API Management returns a stored answer for a prompt that is similar enough, judged against a score threshold, using an embeddings deployment and Azure Managed Redis. A hit skips the model call entirely, a miss pays for the embedding and lookup on top, and a similarity match can return an answer written for a different question, so it suits stable, repeated questions. Priority processing changes the service lane on a standard deployment, at a higher per-token rate. Provisioned throughput reserves capacity and gives the lowest variance under steady load. They combine well: prompt caching on every call, semantic caching where answers repeat, and one capacity option for the latency target. A likely question: does semantic caching break personalization? It can, so include tenant, user and prompt version in the cache scope, as the Well-Architected guidance for AI workloads advises.

scenes.title: Optimization path
scenes.subtitle: Five phases from a measured baseline to governed latency budgets, cheapest changes first.
prove: Streaming reaches the client without buffering
Generated tokens explain the slow requests
Fewer model calls in series keep quality
Capacity option meets the percentile target
scenes.notes: The path orders changes by cost and risk. Phase one measures: a baseline per user journey with timestamps at every hop, percentiles paired with token counts, and streaming configured as in production. Phase two takes the quick wins that need no redesign: streaming from model to client without buffering, output caps and low verbosity, the lowest reasoning effort that passes evaluation, and a stable prompt prefix for caching. Phase three changes the design: the simplest orchestration pattern, a model per agent role, parallel tool calls and minimal retrieval effort. Phase four covers capacity and platform: priority processing or provisioned throughput, separate deployments per workload, co-located regions, and gateway caching where answers repeat. Phase five governs: latency budgets in release gates, continuous evaluation on sampled traffic, and alerts on percentiles. The four checks at the bottom are what to prove first, because each one decides whether the next phase is needed. Order matters: buying capacity before reducing sequential calls and output tokens pays for time that design changes would remove. A likely question: what gives the fastest visible improvement? End-to-end streaming, because it changes when the user sees the first words.
